column2: A survey published in two thousand seven tested two hundred seventy-seven internal medicine residents in Connecticut. Eighty-eight percent felt at least fairly confident about p-values.
Only about fifty-nine percent picked the answer marked correct. A later paper argued even that answer is wrong.
Your test comes back positive. It gives a false alarm to five percent of people without the disease.
So is there a ninety-five percent chance you have it?
Count people instead. Ten thousand of them, and one in a hundred has the disease.
That's one row of a hundred. Say the test catches ninety.
The other nine thousand nine hundred don't have it. Five percent of them still test positive. Four hundred ninety-five false alarms.
Now gather everyone who tested positive.
Ninety have the disease, and four hundred ninety-five don't. So only about fifteen percent of the positives have it.
Five percent was a share of people without the disease. Your question is a share of people who tested positive.
